title: The Surprisingly Swift Decline of US Manufacturing Employment
research_question: Did the removal of uncertainty about future US tariffs on Chinese imports cause the steep decline in US manufacturing employment after 2000? How do industry- and plant-level outcomes — employment, imports, importer entry, and production technology — respond to this shift in trade policy?
data_description: The analysis combines US industry- and plant-level manufacturing data with international trade and tariff information. Key variables include manufacturing employment by industry, US imports from China, counts of US importing firms and foreign-owned Chinese exporters, plant-level labor intensity and production characteristics, and input-output linkages across industries. Tariff variables capture both applied US import tariffs and the statutory 'non-NTR' tariff rates that could have been imposed on Chinese goods absent policy change, with the gap between them measuring industry exposure. The sample spans years before and after 2000, the year the policy change occurred. Comparable European Union industry data are used as a benchmark setting where the analogous policy did not change.
institutional_context: In October 2000, the United States granted China Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR), which took effect upon China's WTO accession in late 2001. Before this change, Chinese imports faced low NTR tariff rates in practice, but these rates required annual renewal by Congress; failure to renew would have triggered a sharp jump to much higher non-NTR (Smoot-Hawley-era) tariffs. PNTR did not lower applied tariffs but permanently eliminated the threat of these large tariff increases, reducing uncertainty for importers and Chinese exporters. Industries varied widely in the size of the gap between NTR and non-NTR rates, generating cross-industry differences in exposure to the policy change. The European Union maintained unchanged trade policy toward China over this period, providing a contrasting setting.
